populist

/POP-yuh-list/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

A populist is a political figure who claims to champion ordinary people against a privileged elite.

The mayor's populist streak showed in every speech — potholes and grocery prices, never a word for the bond markets.

Example

In the 1890s, ruined wheat farmers built a party around a single message — the railroads and the eastern banks were fleecing the plains — and the press called them populists. The label fit: the whole platform was the many against the moneyed few.

A populist stakes out one particular fight: ordinary people against a privileged elite. The word marks that stance, not the speaker's honesty — a populist may be a sincere reformer or a cynical vote-hunter. What it never means is simply 'well liked': plenty of populists lose elections, and plenty of beloved politicians never touch the people-versus-elite theme.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

demagogue: A demagogue whips up the crowd's fears and prejudices, usually with lies, to seize power. A populist claims the people's side against an elite — a stance, not a verdict: a populist's case can be honest.

reformer: A reformer wants the system fixed and may work from any position — expert panels included. A populist adds the frame: the people against the elite, with the speaker on the people's side.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

elitist: someone who sides with the privileged few

technocrat: someone who would rather govern by expert credential than by popular appeal

Where it sits · how far the appeal to 'the people against the elite' is taken

maverick → populist → demagogue

maverick vs. populist: A maverick is a milder figure than a populist: mavericks merely go their own way inside the system, while a populist builds the whole platform on the people's fight against an elite.

demagogue vs. populist: Demagogue goes further than populist — a populist claims the people's cause; a demagogue inflames the crowd's worst fears, usually with falsehoods, to take power for himself.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — popul-: the people (Latin populus)

Suffix — -ist: one who practices or champions

Put it together: Popul- (the people) + -ist (one who champions) = one who champions the people. The name was pinned on America's People's Party in the 1890s and has kept its shape since: a politics that claims 'the people' as its side and names an elite as the enemy.

Use the root in a new word: repopulate: The council's ten-year plan bets everything on repopulating the old mill district.

Root Check

Word Choice

political / analytic — descriptive in history, often charged in headlines

Populist and populace are the pair to keep straight: the populace is the people themselves; a populist is a politician who claims to fight for them. Use populist for the stance — people versus elite — and reach for demagogue only when the method is fear and falsehood. And resist the schoolroom slip: populist never means simply 'popular.'
